trigger: the combat action grid and its submenus
before: Heals. Wasted at full health.
after: Heals 2d10+5 hp, doubled for a Wilmsry, and takes your turn. Greyed out at full health, where it would be wasted.
why: The row never said how much a potion heals or that drinking costs the turn, and it is disabled at full health, so it is never actually wasted there.

trigger: the combat action grid and its submenus
before: Run. They get one swing at your back.
after: Roll to run. Fail and they all get a turn; get away and the loot stays behind.
why: Only a pursuing foe (the Spectre) swings as you leave; the real costs are that a failed roll hands every foe its turn and a clean escape forfeits the loot pile.

trigger: the combat action grid and its submenus
before: Talk it down. An insult is permanent.
after: One try per fight. Fail and they take it personally: every foe hits you and yours one face easier until it ends.
why: The insult lasts only the rest of the fight (C.parleyInsulted, +1 face on every foe swing at the hero and the party), and the one-attempt rule was never stated.

trigger: the combat action grid and its submenus
before: One song per hundred squares. Pick the moment.
after: Sings the best song your level knows, then a hundred squares before the next. Pick the moment.
why: The row gave the cooldown but never said what tapping it does: sing the highest song the Bard's level allows.

trigger: the combat action grid and its submenus
before: Your book holds spells above your level or school. Grow into them.
after: Every spell in your book is above your level or behind your school's level gate. Grow into them.
why: "Above your level or school" does not parse; both locks canCast applies are level gates, which is why growing into them is true of both.

trigger: a foe condition's line on the long-press foe card
before: It swings at where you were a moment ago and almost never lands. A count on the chip is how long until it can see again.
after: It hits only on its die's top face until it can see again: the count on the chip, or the whole fight if there is none. It is swinging at where you were a moment ago.
why: A blind foe swings on exactly one face (foeSwingChain), a spell blindness has no count and lasts the fight, and the line now states that before its flavour.

trigger: a foe condition's line on the long-press foe card
before: Every one of them does half damage while it lasts. They are not taking it well.
after: Every one of them hits on no more than its die's top three faces, and does half damage, while it lasts. They are not taking it well.
why: Weaken also caps every foe swing at three winning faces (C.foeToHitPenalty = 3), which the old line left out; stated in faces because a foe's die scales with its level.

trigger: a hero or member condition chip's tap sheet
before: until something cures it
after: until it runs its course or something cures it
why: Poison and disease also end on their own when their count runs out (engine/movement.js), so a cure is not the only way out.

before: Can't act
why: Verdict on the 77-08 flag: the two-word label said what but not why; the chip now names its kind in one word (Asleep, Stupefied, Maddened; Helpless as the fallback), too short for the corpus, and the tap card opens with "You cannot act".

before: You strike first on a d6. The maze is briefly unfair in your favour.
after: You strike on a d6, the best die there is, while it lasts. The maze is briefly unfair in your favour.
why: Acuteness swaps the strike die to a d6 (strikeDie) and does nothing to who goes first; "strike first" read as initiative.

before: It takes a bite out of you on a schedule. Find a cure before it finds the rest.
after: It takes a few hit points as you walk, but never your last one. That is the nicest thing about it.
why: An affliction ticks hit points on steps and is floored at 1 hp, so the threat of it finding the rest of you was false.

before: You already know what the next encounter is. Whether that helps is up to you.
after: You act first in your next fight, whatever turns up. Whether the warning helps beyond that is up to you.
why: The armed Sense Danger's one mechanical effect is that you act first in the next fight (rollInitiative's foreseen), and the named type is not bound to that fight.

before: Something out there got to you. The next fight opens Afraid — harder to hit, softer blows — until it passes.
after: Something out there got to you: your next fight opens Afraid, −3 to hit and half damage on your blows until it passes, unless Hardiness shrugs it off.
why: "Harder to hit" read as a defence buff; Afraid is −3 to your own hit and half your damage, and Hardiness can shrug it off.

before: They need two better to land a blow, and they know it.
after: Every foe has two fewer faces that hit you, and they know it.
why: ROLL-LEDGER (g) handoff: "need two better" is the roll-under reading; the Anklet's eff foeToHit −2 removes two winning faces, matching its 79-05 item text.

before: You understand them perfectly. Whether that helps is up to them.
after: You can try a parley with anything but the Magical and the Walking Dead, and the roll gets two more faces. Whether they listen is up to them.
why: The Helm's fluency opens parley with every talkative family and adds two faces to the roll (2 × fluency); the old line gave no result.

before: Weightless plate over whatever you wear. It still will not make you graceful.
after: You soak blows as plate, or as your own armour if that is better, and none of it wears out. It still will not make you graceful.
why: armorSoak takes the better of plate and the worn armour and consumes no durability; "over whatever you wear" read as stacking.

before: The round goes on without you. Nothing wakes you early, and foes hit you exactly as they would if you could still swing back.
after: You cannot act: the round goes on without you. Nothing wakes you early, and foes hit you exactly as they would if you could still swing back.
why: With the chip now naming the kind (Asleep, Stupefied, Maddened), its tap card opens with the fact the old label carried.

before: Only the very best swing of the die lands.
after: Only your die's top face lands.
why: "The very best swing of the die" is stilted; the scaling strike die speaks in faces (the ROLL-04 phrasing rule).

before: The next blow that lands on you does half damage. Planning ahead, for once.
after: The next blow that lands does half damage. Planning ahead, for once.
why: A party member's Brace chip reads this same sentence in YOUR LOT, where "on you" named the wrong body.

before: The song is still ringing in everyone's ears, so every swing lands a little easier.
after: Your song is still ringing in your ears: your own strikes land one face easier. The party is pretending not to have heard it.
why: The level-2 song adds one face to the hero's own toHit only; memberToHit never reads it, so "everyone" and "every swing" were wrong.
